newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela calls for Safrica unity, vows more growth.
newsitem.headline: Mandela calls for Safrica unity, vows more growth.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela opened the first parliamentary session under South Africa's new democratic constitution on Friday with a plea for unity and a vow to promote economic growth.

"A new nation is being forged, a nation whose new patriotism and sense of pride derive not only from ideals in our hearts, but also from concrete progress in improving the well-being of all," Mandela said.

Mandela, 78, due to step down when the next election is held in 1999, said his African National Congress had made giant strides in redressing the legacy of apartheid but added that major reforms, particularly in the bloated civil service, were still needed.
"We have laid the foundation for a peaceful and prosperous nation," he said, referring to the constitution that took effect at midnight on Monday after nearly four years of negotiations.
"But it is just that, a foundation. And it will not amount to much if its provisions are not felt in the daily life of our people."
Financial markets responded favourably to the 90-minute speech in which Mandela recommitted his three-year-old government to privatisation and a gradual scrapping of foreign exchange controls.
He said a macro-economic plan to achieve six percent growth and substantial job creation by the year 2000 was in high gear, with privatisation "a critical part" of the programme.
"I would also like to reaffirm our commitment to the phased removal of remaining exchange controls," he said in a remark welcomed in the markets.

The rand, which began strengthening last month after losing nearly 30 percent of its value against the dollar last year, made further gains on Mandela's speech and at 1130 GMT was trading at around 4.44 to the dollar -- its best level in over six months.

Mandela praised the work of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, charged with uncovering human rights abuses from the apartheid era, and urged opposition parties to join the ANC in burying the bitterness of the past.

"I am confident that this united nation we are building is already emerging, and it is the hope that we all have that in due course we will be able to identify the issues on which we should speak with one voice," Mandela said.
He promised tough action against crime, which has become possibly the most pressing social issue.

"Let me warn the criminals, especially the car hijackers, the drug syndicates...the rapists and child abusers... we will continue to escalate the offensive against them, we will make their life really difficult this year," Mandela said.

Outside parliament, separate groups of demonstrators held protests against the government's perceived mishandling of AIDS policy and in favour of the legalisation of marijuana. A total of about 40 people were arrested.

Mandela, whose ANC won a 62 percent landslide in South Africa's first all-race election in April 1994, was at pains to spell out his government's record in providing water, housing, electricity and health facilities to the impoverished black masses.

"During the course of this year we shall further speed up the process of practical implementation. South Africa must become a beehive of communities acting to change their lives for the better," he said.
